771.title: The camel's choice
771.hook: every family wants him as guest, and he lets the camel choose, and it kneels near Abu Ayyub's house (sirah)
771.howItsDone: Muslims retell the camel's kneeling from the sirah and Sahih al-Bukhari when speaking of the founding of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, and honor Abu Ayyub al-Ansari as his host.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mosque at Quba, and a Friday prayer on the road. Your line was: the first friday. Did a gathering make it onto your calendar? Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Who gets the guest? That is the question in the streets of Yathrib as the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, rides in. The city has invited him. Now household after household along the way wants him under its own roof. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, one clan after another steps out and takes hold of the camel's rein: stay with us, we have numbers, we have strength, we will protect you. Any answer he gives will honor one family and pass over the rest, on his very first day. Today: the camel's choice.
screen: `WHO GETS THE GUEST?` → `HANDS ON THE REIN.` → `EVERY ANSWER PASSES SOMEONE OVER.`

segments.voice: His answer, as Ibn Ishaq tells it, is gentle and simple. Let her go her way, he says of the camel, for she is under command. So the rein is let go, and the camel walks on through the town with everyone watching. Bukhari picks up the scene from there. The camel kneels at a spot in the city, an open place where dates were spread out to dry, belonging to two orphan boys. And the Prophet says: this, if Allah wills, is the place to stay. Then he does something careful. He calls the two boys and asks to buy the land for a mosque. They say, in effect: no, we'll give it to you. He refuses the gift and pays for it. On that ground the mosque of Medina is built, and in the meantime he lodges nearby, in the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. Muslim's collection preserves a small scene from those days: Abu Ayyub, living upstairs, can't bear to walk above the Prophet's head, and asks him to move to the upper floor. Consider what the camel spared everyone. No clan could say: he chose them over us. No one had to win. The choice was left to the camel, which, in his words, was under command, and he passed over no family himself. Then see what happened next: once the place was found, he didn't just take it. He paid two orphans what it was worth. Letting go of choosing did not mean letting go of care.
screen: `LET HER GO, SHE IS UNDER COMMAND.` · `THE CAMEL KNEELS.` · `HE PAYS THE TWO ORPHANS.` · `NO CLAN PASSED OVER.` · then, large: `LET THE CAMEL CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: let go of choosing once. Settle, and breathe. Think of a small decision on your plate today where several good options are tugging at you, and where it doesn't much matter which one wins. Where to eat, which friend to call first, which task to start. Notice your hands on the rein. Now loosen them. Decide that today you'll let something else choose: the first one that comes along, the one someone else prefers, the one that's nearest. If you pray, you can hand the choice to Allah. Feel your grip ease. The bell holds the time.
Abu Ayyub. In whose house the Prophet lodged near the spot where the camel, under command, chose to kneel. Today's word.
Your line: let the camel choose. Today, hand one small choice away, and see whose feelings it spares. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: The people of the bench
772.hook: poor companions live on a shaded platform in the mosque, learning (Bukhari)
772.howItsDone: Muslims remember ahl al-suffah as a model of learning and of caring for the poor, and some mosques and schools support students who live and study on site.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the camel knelt near Abu Ayyub's house, on two orphans' land. Your line was: let the camel choose. Which small choice did you hand away? Day seven hundred seventy-two.

Too many hadith. Some people grumbled that Abu Hurayra reported too many sayings of the Prophet. That complaint is old enough to be answered inside Sahih al-Bukhari, by Abu Hurayra himself. His answer is about where he spent his days. His brothers among the emigrants, he says, were busy with trading in the markets. His brothers among the people of Medina were busy working their property. And he stayed close to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, content with whatever filled his stomach, present when others were away, remembering what others forgot. He had a place to stay close. Today: ahl al-suffah, the people of the bench.
screen: `TOO MANY HADITH?` → `OTHERS IN THE MARKET.` → `HE STAYED CLOSE.`

segments.voice: When the mosque of Medina was built, part of it had a covered, shaded platform. The Arabic word is suffah, and the people who lived there were called ahl al-suffah, the people of the suffah, the people of the bench. Who were they? Bukhari has Abu Hurayra describe them in another report: the guests of Islam, people with no family to go to and no wealth to fall back on. The bench was their home, and the mosque was their school. Bukhari also shows how they were fed. When charity came to the Prophet, he sent it to them and took none of it himself. When a gift came, he shared in it with them. In one long report, Abu Hurayra is so hungry he can barely stand, and the Prophet sends him to call the people of the bench to share a single bowl of milk. Abu Hurayra worries there will be nothing left for him. He serves them all, and in that story there's enough. The arrangement says something. The community put the people with the least in the middle of the mosque itself. Not at the edge of town. Not out of sight. In the mosque, beside the teaching. And the poor were not only receivers. Because they stayed, they listened. Because they listened, they remembered. And Abu Hurayra, who stayed close while others were busy, became the man people asked why he had so many sayings to report.
screen: `A SHADED PLATFORM IN THE MOSQUE.` · `THE GUESTS OF ISLAM.` · `CHARITY SENT TO THEM.` · `THE POOR WHO REMEMBERED.` · then, large: `THE BENCH OF THE POOR.`

segments.voice: The practice: give to students. Breathe slowly and settle. Bring to mind someone who is learning right now and doesn't have much: a student you know, a young person in your family, someone retraining, someone studying their faith. Picture them on that bench. What would help them stay close to what they're learning? A meal, a book, a little money, your time, a word of encouragement. Choose one small thing you could actually give this week. If you pray, you can ask Allah to open their way. Keep their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ahl al-suffah. The people of the bench: poor companions who lived on the shaded platform of the mosque in Medina, fed by charity, learning close to the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: the bench of the poor. Today, make room for one learner who has little, and give them something that helps them stay. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

773.title: "Show me the market"
773.hook: offered half his brother's wealth, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf asks only to be shown the market (Bukhari)
773.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' when speaking of the brotherhood (mu'akhah) between the emigrants and the Ansar, and of earning an honest living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people of the bench, poor companions living in the mosque. Your line was: the bench of the poor. Which learner came to mind, and what could you give them? Day seven hundred seventy-three.

Two strangers, made brothers. When the emigrants arrived in Medina with almost nothing, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, paired them up with the people of the city. Newcomers were given local brothers. Bukhari keeps one of those pairings in the newcomer's own words. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, from Mecca, is paired with Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', from Medina. And Sa'd, almost at once, makes him an enormous offer. Today: show me the market.
screen: `STRANGERS MADE BROTHERS.` → `ABD AL-RAHMAN AND SA'D.` → `AN OFFER ON THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Sa'd says, in Abd al-Rahman's telling: I am the wealthiest of the Ansar. I will divide my wealth in half, and half is yours. Weigh that offer. This is not a meal or a loan. It is half of everything, given to a man he has just met, because the Prophet called them brothers. Abd al-Rahman's answer is the line we're carrying today. He says, in effect: I have no need of that. Is there a market here where trade goes on? Sa'd tells him: the market of Qaynuqa. The next morning Abd al-Rahman is there. He buys and sells dried curd and clarified butter, small goods, and keeps going back day after day. Before long, Bukhari says, he turns up with a trace of yellow perfume on him, the sign of a bridegroom. He has earned enough to marry. Look at the two men side by side. Neither of them is the hero alone. Sa'd's generosity is real and total: he offered half, and meant it. Abd al-Rahman's refusal is not pride. He answers with thanks, and with a blessing on Sa'd's family and wealth. What he asks for instead is a door: not the money, but the place where money is honestly made. Both are kindness. One gives. The other protects the giver, and keeps his own dignity. The brotherhood stayed whole, and so did both men's dignity.
screen: `HALF OF EVERYTHING IS YOURS.` · `IS THERE A MARKET HERE?` · `CURD AND BUTTER, DAY AFTER DAY.` · `ONE GIVES, ONE PROTECTS THE GIVER.` · then, large: `SHOW ME THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: The practice: earn something honestly. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think about your work, paid or unpaid, and the way you earn what you have. Notice one place where it's honest and clean, and let yourself be glad of it. Then notice one place that could be cleaner: a shortcut, an exaggeration, a corner cut. Don't argue with it. Just see it. Choose one small thing you'll do today to earn your keep straight. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless what you earn. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Qaynuqa, the market Sa'd sent him to, where Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf earned his own way instead of taking half his new brother's wealth. Today's word.
Your line: a trace of yellow perfume. Today, when someone offers to carry you, thank them, and ask for the door instead. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

774.title: The charter
774.hook: the Medina charter makes the city's tribes, including its Jewish tribes, one community for defense
774.howItsDone: Muslims and historians study the charter of Medina (al-sahifah), preserved in Ibn Ishaq's sirah and other early works, and some Muslims point to it today when they speak of living alongside people of other faiths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf turned down half his brother's wealth. Your line was: a trace of yellow perfume. What did you earn straight? Day seven hundred seventy-four.

Clan after clan, written down one by one. That is how the document reads. Medina was not an empty town waiting for newcomers. It held Arab clans with old feuds between them, Jewish tribes with their own long histories there, and now emigrants from Mecca, newly arrived and far from home. Any of them could ask: whose city is this now? Who protects whom? Who pays when someone is hurt? The sirah of Ibn Ishaq preserves a written answer, drawn up under the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Today: the charter.
screen: `CLAN AFTER CLAN.` → `OLD FEUDS, NEW ARRIVALS.` → `WHOSE CITY IS THIS NOW?`

segments.voice: As Ibn Ishaq gives it, the charter opens by naming the believers of Quraysh and of Yathrib, and those who join them and strive alongside them, and declares that they are one community, one ummah. Then it gets practical. It goes clan by clan: each one keeps its old customs for paying blood money and ransoming its captives, fairly and kindly. No one is to leave a debtor stranded. Then it turns to the Jewish tribes of the city. In Ibn Ishaq's text, the Jews of the clan of Awf are named a community alongside the believers: to the Jews their religion, and to the believers theirs. Other Jewish clans are named in the same way. Each side bears its own expenses. They are to help one another against anyone who attacks the people of the document. They owe one another sincere advice. And the valley of Yathrib is declared sacred for the people of the document. What kind of unity is this? It does not make everyone the same. Each clan keeps its customs. Each religion keeps its own practice. The word one is used, but it is a one made of many named parts, each listed, none erased. What binds them is a promise: to defend the city together, and to bring disputes to God and to Muhammad, not to the old feuds. Some historians ask how the text came together and when, and the city's later story has hard chapters ahead. But the document itself, as preserved, names party after party and gives each a place.
screen: `ONE UMMAH, NAMED CLAN BY CLAN.` · `EACH KEEPS ITS CUSTOMS.` · `TO THE JEWS THEIR RELIGION.` · `DEFEND THE CITY TOGETHER.` · then, large: `ONE COMMUNITY OF MANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: make an agreement fair to all. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group you belong to where things are a little unclear or a little unfair: a household, a team, a group of friends, a shared apartment. Who carries more than their share? Whose way of doing things gets ignored? In your mind, write it down like the charter, party by party. Name each person. Give each one a fair part to carry, and let each keep what matters to them. If you pray, you can ask Allah for fairness among you. Choose one line you could actually propose. The bell holds the time.

The charter. The agreement of Medina, preserved by Ibn Ishaq, that names the city's believers and its Jewish tribes, clan by clan, as one community for defense, each keeping its own religion. Today's word.
Your line: one community of many. Today, in one group you're part of, name everyone's share out loud, and make sure no one is left out of the list. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

775.title: The turning qiblah
775.hook: at the mosque of the two qiblahs, the prayer turns mid-way from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:144)
775.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'bah in Mecca for every prayer, wherever they are, and a mosque's niche (mihrab) marks the qiblah; in Medina, visitors pray at the mosque known as the mosque of the two qiblahs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the charter of Medina, the city's clans named one by one. Your line was: one community of many. Who did you make sure was on the list? Day seven hundred seventy-five.

A row of people, bowed in prayer, and a voice at the door. Bukhari tells it like this. A man who had just prayed with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks past another mosque where people are in the middle of their prayer, bent over, facing toward Jerusalem. And he calls out: I bear witness that I have just prayed with the Messenger of Allah facing Mecca. And they turn. Right there, in the middle of the prayer, as they are. Today: qiblah.
screen: `A VOICE AT THE DOOR.` → `FACING JERUSALEM.` → `THEY TURN, AS THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: The qiblah is the direction Muslims face in prayer. In Medina, the early Muslims had been praying toward Jerusalem. Bukhari says the Prophet loved that his qiblah would be the Ka'bah in Mecca, the house tradition says Abraham raised. And the Qur'an, in surah two, speaks of the turning of his face toward heaven, as if waiting. Then the verse comes. In Pickthall's words, in surah two, verse one hundred forty-four: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." The same verse says the believers too, wherever they are, are to turn their faces toward it. Now go back to that mosque. The news arrives mid-prayer. Nobody stops to hold a meeting. Nobody says, let's finish this one the old way and start fresh tomorrow. They turn, in the rows, as they are. Bukhari has a second report of the people of Quba hearing it at the dawn prayer and doing the same. Tradition remembers one of these places as the mosque of the two qiblahs, a mosque where a single prayer was offered facing two directions. Then there's the prayer itself. Its first half wasn't wrong. It was prayed in obedience, facing where they'd been told. The second half was too. What made both halves one prayer was not the direction. It was the turning: being ready to change where you face the moment the call comes, without leaving the prayer.
screen: `THE DIRECTION OF PRAYER.` · `HIS FACE TURNED TOWARD HEAVEN.` · `THE VERSE: TURN THY FACE.` · `ONE PRAYER, TWO DIRECTIONS.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: face the qiblah with fresh eyes. If you know where Mecca lies from where you're sitting, turn gently toward it now. If you don't, simply choose to sit facing one direction on purpose. Settle, and breathe. Notice that your whole body is pointed somewhere. Then think of one thing in your day you've been facing out of habit, and ask whether it's time to turn. Not to throw away what came before. Just to turn. If you pray, you can ask Allah to keep your face toward Him. Stay facing. The bell holds the time.
Qiblah. The direction of prayer that changed from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah in Mecca, and worshipers turned toward it in the middle of their prayer. Today's word.
Your line: turn to the house. Today, when you notice you're facing the wrong way in something, turn right there, mid-way, without waiting to start over. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

776.title: Badr: the night rain
776.hook: before Badr, Allah sends sleep for calm and rain to firm the ground (8:11)
776.howItsDone: Muslims read surah al-Anfal (8) for the story of Badr, and some recite the Prophet's bedtime remembrances before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the qiblah turned, and people turned with it in the middle of prayer. Your line was: turn to the house. Where did you turn mid-way? Day seven hundred seventy-six.

The night before a fight the Muslims had not set out for. The Muslims of Medina had ridden out after a trading caravan from Mecca. The caravan slipped away along the coast, and instead an army from Mecca was coming to meet them, at a place of wells called Badr. Now they are camped in a sandy valley, outnumbered, the battle set for morning. A night like that is made for lying awake, running through what might happen. Surah eight remembers what happened that night instead. Today: Badr.
screen: `A CARAVAN SLIPS AWAY.` → `AN ARMY COMING INSTEAD.` → `THE NIGHT BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Surah eight, verse eleven, speaks to the believers about that night. It opens, in Pickthall's words: "When He made the slumber fall upon you as a reassurance from Him." Slumber: a drowsiness that comes down over anxious people and lets them rest. The verse calls it a reassurance, sent from Allah. Then it goes on: He sent down water from the sky. The same verse gives the rain its jobs: to purify them, to take from them a taint of Satan, to strengthen their hearts, and to make their feet firm. Ibn Ishaq fills in the ground-level picture. The valley was soft sand. The rain packed it down where the Muslims were, so they could walk and stand on it, while the same rain made the going heavy for the army on the other side. One night, one rain, and the ground under their feet changed. Some reports add another picture. In Musnad Ahmad, Ali says that on the night of Badr everyone slept except the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who stood praying under a tree until morning. So the story holds both: a camp of people given sleep, and one man awake on their behalf. Notice the order inside that one verse. It doesn't speak of swords. It speaks of sleep, then rain, and only then of firm feet. Before anyone is asked to stand, they are given rest, and the ground is made ready for their feet. Rest first. Then stand.
screen: `SLUMBER AS A REASSURANCE.` · `RAIN TO MAKE THE FEET FIRM.` · `SOFT SAND PACKED DOWN.` · `ONE MAN AWAKE, PRAYING.` · then, large: `SLEEP, THEN STAND.`

segments.voice: The practice: sleep well before a hard day. Sit or lie back, and let your shoulders drop. Think of the next hard day ahead of you, a meeting, a conversation, an exam, a long shift. Notice the part of you that wants to stay up rehearsing it. Then picture rain falling on soft sand and packing it firm, while you sleep. You don't have to do that part. Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in. If you pray, you can ask Allah for calm and for firm ground. Let your body feel heavy. The bell holds the time.
Badr. The place of wells where the Muslims camped the night before a great test, and where, the Qur'an says, Allah sent slumber for calm and rain to make their feet firm. Today's word.
Your line: sleep, then stand. Tonight, before whatever is hard tomorrow, stop rehearsing at a set time and go to bed. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

777.title: Badr: the day
777.hook: about three hundred against a thousand, two young men of the Ansar in the row, and the Meccan leaders fall (Muslim; Bukhari)
777.howItsDone: Muslims retell Badr in sermons and sirah classes, and the Qur'an's own reminder of it in Surah Al Imran and Surah al-Anfal is recited in prayer like any other passage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Badr, the night before: sleep sent down for calm, and rain to firm the sand. Your line was: sleep, then stand. Did you get some rest before something hard? Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

Morning, by the wells. In a report in Sahih Muslim, Umar says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ looked across at the Meccan army, a thousand men, and then at his own companions, a little over three hundred. He turned toward the qiblah and raised his hands. That's where the day begins. By the time it ends, Meccan leaders who had set themselves against the new faith are among the dead, and a small band that expected to be crushed is still standing. Today: Badr, the day itself.
screen: `A THOUSAND.` → `A LITTLE OVER THREE HUNDRED.` → `HANDS RAISED TOWARD THE QIBLAH.`

segments.voice: A very human report of the battle comes from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market a few days ago. In Sahih al-Bukhari he says he was standing in the row, and he looked to his right and to his left, and found two young men of the Ansar beside him. He admits he wished for stronger men at his sides. Then one of them nudged him and whispered: uncle, do you know Abu Jahl? What do you want with him, Abd al-Rahman asked. I've heard he insults the Messenger of Allah, the young man said. Then the other one nudged him and asked the very same thing. When Abd al-Rahman pointed him out, both went straight for him, and they struck him down. Afterward each came to the Prophet saying he had done it. The Prophet looked at their two swords and said: both of you killed him. The two he had wished away were the two who went straight for him. Later, Surah Al Imran looks back on that day, and it doesn't flatter anyone. In Pickthall's words: "Allah had already given you the victory at Badr, when ye were contemptible." Contemptible is a strong old word. It means small, weak, easy to look down on. The verse goes on: so keep your duty to Allah, that you may be thankful. Surah al-Anfal says something close: remember when you were few, counted weak in the land, afraid that people would snatch you away, and He gave you refuge and strengthened you. So these two verses tell Badr less as a triumph than as a rescue. The point isn't how strong they were. It's how small they were, and where the thanks should go.
screen: `TWO YOUNG MEN OF THE ANSAR.` · `BOTH OF YOU KILLED HIM.` · `WHEN YE WERE CONTEMPTIBLE.` · `THAT YOU MAY BE THANKFUL.` · then, large: `FEW AGAINST MANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: give thanks for a rescue, and for who it came through. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring back one time you were outnumbered: by bills, by a deadline, by a diagnosis, by a room that was against you. Now look to your right and your left in that memory. Who was standing beside you that you didn't expect much from? A younger colleague, a neighbor, a kid who said the right thing. Let their face come clear. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, for the rescue. If you don't, just hold that person in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Badr: the wells where a little over three hundred met a thousand, and the place the Qur'an names when it reminds the Muslims they were once small, and rescued. Today's word.

Your line: few against many. This week walked from a camel kneeling in Medina, past a bench of poor students, a market, a charter and a turning qiblah, to the wells. Today, tell one person you didn't expect much from that they helped you. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the place, with its wells, where the battle was fought; the Qur'an names it in 3:123.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle won by strength.
what it means: few against many, told as a rescue that calls for thanks.
what a scholar hears: 3:123's 'when ye were contemptible', 8:26's few and feeble, and Bukhari's two young Ansar.
